topic.title: How NVIDIA's first chip, the NV1, drew 3D with curved patches instead of triangles, lost to DirectX's triangles, and how the triangle chip that followed saved the company

title: What Was Wrong With NVIDIA's First Chip?
description:
Why did almost no game use NVIDIA's first graphics card?
We build its chip in 3D and set its curved patches beside the triangles every other chip drew, then follow how DirectX settled the fight and what NVIDIA built next.
Sources: Jon Peddie Research, SiliconANGLE (Jan 2026).
Animations are simplified illustrations, not exact to scale.
cta: Curves or triangles: which would you have bet on? Comment

lines.text: Almost no game could use NVIDIA's first graphics card.
Its chip packed about 250K transistors and bet everything on curves.
Bend one flat sheet into a smooth dome: a single patch, round edges.
Other chips cut that dome into flat triangles. More pieces, each easy to draw.
Which would games use? Microsoft built DirectX, the Windows games toolkit, around triangles.
Game makers chose triangles, and NVIDIA struggled to stay in business.
NVIDIA threw the curves away. Its next chip, RIVA, drew triangles fast: 3.5M transistors.
It sold, and NVIDIA never looked back. Today its newest chip, Rubin, packs 336B transistors.
Curves or triangles: which would you pick? NVIDIA learned the hard way.

Re-review of the shortened beats (bet, curves, triangles, directx, shelf, turn, payoff, loop; say and spoken match, figures still {fact1}/{fact4}/{fact5}): 'about 250K transistors and bet everything on curves' (JPR: approx. 250,000, built on quadratic texture mapping), 'NVIDIA struggled to stay in business' (JPR wording), 'RIVA drew triangles fast: 3.5M transistors' and 'It sold, and NVIDIA never looked back' (JPR: put Nvidia back on the map, generated revenue), Rubin 336B still NVIDIA's newest chip; 'Other chips' is softer than before. Facts confirmed earlier on source pages. Notes: 'next chip' skips the unreleased NV2 (RIVA 128 is NV3); 'bet everything' is rhetorical (the NV1 also did 2D and audio); 'built DirectX around triangles' is simplified.

Re-render fixes all four notes: RIVA (40s) is a lidded chip distinct from NV1's open die, 45s 'It sold' is a store shelf of game-pad boxes, the DirectX PC sits inside the frame with the Microsoft logo writing on at 25s, game boxes carry game-pad prints at 0s/30s, 250K plate beside the dome at 10s; first frame names NVIDIA with the real NV1 card, loop and pick-one close fine, layout/craft empty, audio -1.0/-16.9 dB, thumbnail clear. Minor: Rubin's die at 50s reuses the NV1 die texture (the tiny-chip scale shot lands after the sampled still).

All 5 facts confirmed on source pages: NV1 ~250,000 transistors and NVIDIA founded early 1993 (JPR/Electronic Design 2021-06-22); $250 2 MB board, RIVA 128 3.5M transistors, 'struggling to stay in business', DirectX push around triangle rendering (JPR/Electronic Design RIVA 128); Rubin 336B (SiliconANGLE 2026-01-05, and NVIDIA's own developer blog 'Inside the NVIDIA Rubin Platform'). Verify list: quadratic texture mapping (JPR, Wikipedia NV1); Edge 3D with Saturn controller ports (search: Wikipedia, TechSpot); DirectX 1.0 on 1995-09-30 (Heise, Britannica); Rubin is still NVIDIA's newest shipping GPU (Rubin Ultra 2027, Feynman 2028 are roadmap only). No advice, no hype, disclaimer ends the description. Notes: the NV1 card was sold by Diamond (Edge 3D), so 'NVIDIA's first graphics card' is loose; DirectX 1.0 had no Direct3D (it came in DirectX 2.0, 1996), so 'built DirectX around triangles' is simplified; 'every other chip' drew triangles holds for PC chips (the Saturn drew quads).
